summary: Explains how clients should navigate a Whois++ mesh, where each server refers the client onward to the next appropriate servers. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: If you ask one librarian and they point you to another, you follow the pointers. This explains how a program follows those pointers through a web of directory servers.

questions: how to query a whois++ mesh
how do whois++ clients navigate the mesh
what is the directory of servers in whois++
how do whois++ clients detect loops
when should a whois++ client expand a search
subtitle: How clients navigate a distributed mesh of directory servers.

tldr.problem: A distributed directory service needs a way for clients to navigate across multiple servers, each referring the client to other servers as needed.
tldr.mechanism: Clients track which servers they have queried and follow server referrals, detecting loops themselves while expanding searches to cover the entire mesh.
tldr.outcome: This standards-track protocol defined in 1996 specified practical algorithms for mesh navigation, but the Whois++ system is now historic and has been superseded by other directory technologies.

today: RFC 1914 is Historic and is no longer used. The Whois++ architecture it describes has been superseded by other directory service technologies. Modern directory lookups use different protocols and architectural approaches.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1914 defines how clients should interact with a Whois++ mesh, a distributed architecture of directory servers. In Whois++, each server is responsible for a portion of the data and refers clients to other servers that might have the information they are looking for.

The RFC establishes that the client, not the servers, bears the responsibility for navigating this mesh. When a client queries a server and receives referrals to other servers, the client must decide which servers to contact next, keep track of where it has already searched, and detect loops in the mesh structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one big directory, Whois++ is like a network of librarians. Your client (the person searching) has to remember who you have already asked and follow the pointers they give you.

sections.title: The Whois++ Mesh Architecture
sections.content:
The Whois++ mesh is composed of multiple servers arranged in a hierarchical structure, though not necessarily a strict tree. Servers are configured with knowledge of other servers they know about, and they can refer clients to additional servers to search.

Each client is configured with a default Whois++ server, usually chosen to be as local as possible given the client's location and the type of information (template) being sought. The simplest interaction is straightforward: the client connects to a server, sends a query, receives an answer, and closes the connection. If the answer contains hits, it is presented to the user. If the server returns pointers to other servers to ask, the client can automatically follow those pointers.

One key feature of the mesh is that servers can be queried by multiple parent servers, so the same server can participate in multiple hierarchies at once. This flexibility requires clients to detect and avoid loops on their own.
sections.plainLanguage: Different library branches know about each other, and each librarian has a list of other branches that might have what you are looking for. You have to keep track of which branches you have already visited.

sections.title: Navigating the Mesh: Expansion Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC describes the primary client strategy: when a search returns zero hits or when a user wants to expand the search, the client should issue polled-by and polled-for queries to the current server. These queries return the addresses of other servers in the mesh that might have more information. The client then repeats the original query to those new servers.

To prevent infinite loops, the client must maintain a QueriedServers set that tracks every server it has already contacted. Before querying a server, the client checks if that server is already in this set. If it is, the client skips it, avoiding the loop.

The RFC provides a detailed algorithm showing how the client manages three lists: the current server list, the set of already-queried servers, and the growing answer list. The algorithm loops until all reachable servers in the mesh have been queried or expansion is stopped. This approach causes clients to progressively query larger and more comprehensive index servers, with each layer of the mesh providing knowledge that helps prune unnecessary branches.
sections.plainLanguage: When you do not find an answer at your first library, ask which other libraries are nearby and ask them the same question. But write down which libraries you have already asked so you do not ask the same one twice.

sections.title: The Directory of Servers
sections.content:
While the expansion algorithm works well, RFC 1914 also describes a complementary service called the Directory of Servers. This is a special Whois++ server that polls every other Whois++ server in the system to maintain information about what records each server holds.

A client can query the Directory of Servers to find which servers hold particular types of information. For example, a client seeking all Whois++ servers that serve user templates in a specific country can query the Directory and receive a list of serverhandle records. Each record contains the server's handle, hostname, port number, and optionally the administrator's contact information, organization name, and description.

In the current protocol version, querying the Directory of Servers requires the client to be pre-configured with its hostname and port. The RFC notes that this lookup should not be fully automatic in the client; instead, it is intended to help users find a better starting point for their search, though future versions might automate this selection.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a special librarian who knows about all the other libraries. You can ask them which libraries have the kind of book you are looking for.

sections.title: Caching and Resilience
sections.content:
Clients can cache information they receive from servers, including records, IP addresses of Whois++ servers, and the address of the Directory of Servers. Each client can choose how long to cache each piece of information.

The RFC addresses a practical problem: when a server returns a referral with a hostname and port number, that information may be stale. If the connection to that server fails, the client can fall back to the Directory of Servers and look up the server by its handle to get the current hostname and port.

The RFC also recommends that clients maintain a blacklist of servers they should not query, in case a fake Whois++ server is discovered. Additionally, since an expanding query can take a long time and consume significant resources, clients should be able to stop mid-search, and more sophisticated clients should be able to configure cost limits to avoid expensive servers.
sections.plainLanguage: You can remember the phone numbers of libraries you have called before. If a phone number does not work anymore, you can look up the library's current number. You can also avoid calling libraries that are too expensive or that you do not trust.
